generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, this shows up across every subject you study. After an essay, a project, a presentation or a placement, you are expected to look back and ask not just what you did but how you worked. Early on the habit is easy to skip, because nothing forces you to do it. Making that honest look-back a deliberate step, in any field, is what turns an experience into something you actually learn from.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students who have just had the same piece of work returned with a middling mark and some feedback.

{{learner-a}} reads the feedback, notes that the mark was lower than hoped, and writes: 'I got 58. The marker said my argument was unclear and I lost marks on structure. I will try harder next time.' This records what happened and ends with a vague intention. It is a description, not a reflection: it never asks why the argument was unclear, or what 'trying harder' would actually involve.

{{learner-b}} reads the same feedback and looks back honestly. 'My argument was unclear because I started writing before I had settled on a line, so each paragraph pulled a different way. The structure slipped because I left planning until too late. Next time I will fix my argument in one sentence first, and outline the sections before I draft.' This is reflection: it asks why things went as they did and turns that into specific, doable changes.

Both students looked back at the same work. Only {{learner-b}} moved past describing it to learning from it.
generatedProse.summary: Reflection is a deliberate, honest look back at your work, so that you can learn from it rather than simply describe what happened. You can now explain what reflection is, recognise it in how a student looks back on a piece of work, and say why it matters: it is how a self-directed learner turns experience into improvement, in any subject. The next lesson gives you a simple model for doing it.

check.body: In the worked example, what made {{learner-b}}'s log a reflection rather than a description?

items.text: Asking why the work fell short, and turning it into specific changes.
Recording the mark and the marker's comments accurately.
Promising to try harder next time.

feedback.correct: That's right. Asking why the work fell short and planning specific changes is what makes it a reflection.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look for what {{learner-b}} did beyond recording the feedback.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}} reflected because the log asked why the work fell short and planned specific changes, not because it recorded the feedback accurately or ran longer.

_prompts.concept-context: What does this look like in practice within the given context? Write a short follow-on from the generic definition above, in the learner's own subject or discipline. Keep it to two or three sentences, mid-register, following straight on from the generic definition.
_prompts.worked-example: Give a subject-specific worked example of this lesson's concept: a weaker or less-developed version first, then a stronger version reached by better practice, using the context cast (character tokens) consistently. Keep the weaker-then-stronger shape and the two-part contrast; carry the cast only through the {{learner-a}} (weaker) and {{learner-b}} (stronger) tokens, never a literal name (the pack supplies the whole body, but not the names). Each example paragraph must begin with its token, weaker first - merge-context.js's wrapProse() only emits the we-weaker/we-stronger cue classes for a paragraph that leads with the token. The merge renders it as a block quote, so write it as continuous prose, not as a quoted comment plus commentary.
_prompts.summary: Recap what the learner can now do, in terms of their own subject or context. One short paragraph. Do not restate the learning outcomes verbatim.
_prompts.check: Write the subject's own version of this lesson's check question(s), testing the same outcome in the learner's own discipline. Keep the same number of items and the same correctness pattern as the generic version; reword the stem and items for the subject. Keep the component-level feedback (correct / notFinal / final) teaching, never a bare verdict.
